label: Constitutional Analysis
sentences: The question here falls under Article III, Section 2, Clause 1. The judicial power extends to all cases, in law and equity, arising under the Constitution, the laws of the United States, and treaties; to all cases affecting ambassadors, other public ministers and consuls; to all cases of admiralty and maritime jurisdiction; to controversies to which the United States is a party; to controversies between two or more states, between a state and citizens of another state, between citizens of different states, between citizens of the same state claiming lands under grants of different states, and between a state or its citizens and foreign states, citizens or subjects.
This story is about when a court may end a government lawsuit.

In 1787, the Committee of Detail's report of August 6, 1787 vested the judicial power in one Supreme Court and "in such inferior Courts as shall, when necessary, from time to time, be constituted by the Legislature of the United States."
A federal judge threw out a suit about an Alaska Senate race.
Judge Gleason found the federal government may not bring the suit.
Judge Gleason said a court order would risk the secret ballot.
The strongest argument against this is that this clause covers suits with the government as a party, so ending the case early denies that party the full decision the clause promises.
We read this clause to mean courts may adjudge only real cases and whether a party may sue at all.
This keeps judges on cases and not on the work of other branches.
